Description: ask the patient necessary ice-breaking questions (such as what's the purpose of the visit or any necessary question to make the patient feel comfortable and build connections; these are not related to the symptoms and it is only for ice-breaking) to initiate the interview. the criteria are met when the patient has an elevated or expansive mood
Patient_Story: I have elevated mood. I feel like I am on top of the world. I have been feeling incredibly euphoric, as if I could accomplish anything. I remember staying up late talking with friends, planning an elaborate trip that I impulsively decided we should take, and I even booked the hotel without thinking twice about the cost. However, it all came crashing down when I suddenly felt depressed and withdrawn, barely able to get out of bed for a few days afterward. The stark contrast between those highs and lows has left me feeling a bit confused and concerned about what’s happening to me.

Description: Determine if the patient's elevated or expansive mood is primarily due to the physiological effects of a substance, such as drugs, alcohol, or medications for any medical conditions. The criteria is met when the patient's mood disturbance is directly linked to the substance's effects.
Patient_Story: During the orientation for my art class, I felt inspired and uplifted, like my creative juices were flowing. This wasn't unusual for me; I often experience waves of excitement when I'm pursuing something I love. I’ve made sure to stay away from any substances like alcohol or drugs, so I know my mood is just a natural reaction to the positive changes in my life, not influenced by anything external.

Description: Determine if the patient's elevated or expansive mood is primarily caused by the physiological effects of a general medical condition, such as physical health issues. This assessment should focus on whether the mood disturbance is directly linked to the underlying medical condition.
Patient_Story: Lately, I've been feeling more energetic and euphoric than ever, especially after I got diagnosed with hyperthyroidism. After starting treatment, I noticed how my mood seemed to lift, and I was unusually talkative with my friends at our weekly meet-up. I couldn't contain my enthusiasm, sharing every detail about my art class and how excited I was about life in general. It felt like the changes in my physical health were fueling this elevated mood, almost as if my body was responding to the medication in a way that made everything seem brighter.

Description: Assess whether the patient shows evidence of decline in one or more cognitive domains, including complex attention, executive function, learning and memory, language, perceptual-motor abilities, or social cognition. This decline should be noticeable and impact the patient's ability to function in these specific areas.
Patient_Story: I don't think I've noticed any decline in my cognitive abilities lately. In fact, I've been feeling quite sharp, especially when I’m working on my art projects. Just last week, I had an intense brainstorming session with my classmates where we bounced around ideas for our upcoming exhibition, and I was able to articulate my thoughts clearly and keep up with the discussions without any issues. I feel confident in my memory and focus, which seems to be better than ever since starting my treatment.

Description: Bipolar and Related Disorder due to another medical condition
Patient_Story: I remember the day I went for my follow-up appointment after starting medication for my hyperthyroidism. As I sat in the waiting room, I felt a rush of excitement mixed with these intense mood swings; one moment I was practically bouncing in my seat, talking to anyone who would listen about my art class, and the next, I felt a wave of irritability wash over me, leaving me on edge. My psychiatrist noted that these fluctuations in mood could indeed be linked to my medical condition, which was a bit alarming, but it made sense given how dramatically my emotions shifted throughout the week.

Description: Evaluate if the elevated or expansive mood reported by the patient is the primary focus of the clinical picture and is of sufficient severity to require clinical attention. This means the symptoms should be significant enough to cause notable distress or impairment, making them a central concern in the patient's overall condition.
Patient_Story: While I do experience some periods of heightened enthusiasm, I wouldn’t say my mood is a primary concern. For instance, during our weekly meet-ups, I might feel excited and share my ideas passionately, but I can easily switch back to a calmer state when the conversation shifts. It’s more about riding the waves of my interests, rather than something that distresses me or impairs my daily life.

Description: Substance/Medication-Induced Bipolar Disorder
Patient_Story: I’ve never used substances like alcohol or drugs, and my psychiatrist has assured me that my mood swings are primarily linked to my thyroid condition. For example, just the other day, I was at a café with friends, sharing a laugh one moment and then feeling a bit irritable the next, but it felt connected to my body's fluctuations rather than any external influence. I’ve been proactive about my health, focusing on my treatment and making sure my mood changes are just a part of my journey, not a byproduct of substance use.

Description: Substance Intoxication; Substance Withdrawal; Other Adverse Effect of Medication
Patient_Story: I’ve never experienced any substance intoxication or withdrawal, as I’ve always been careful to avoid alcohol and drugs entirely. In fact, I often feel grateful that I haven't had to deal with any adverse effects from medications, especially since my psychiatrist has managed my hyperthyroidism treatment well. Just the other day, I mentioned to my doctor how I've been feeling energized from the medication without any negative side effects, which reassured me that I’m on the right track.

Description: Major or Mild Neurocognitive disorder due to another medical condition, with behavioral disturbance
Patient_Story: I don't think I've experienced any significant cognitive decline or behavioral disturbances due to my hyperthyroidism. In fact, my focus and memory have both felt sharper since starting treatment, allowing me to engage fully in my art class. I remember discussing intricate techniques with my classmates without any trouble, feeling completely in control of my thoughts and actions during those conversations.

Description: the patient has reported clinically significant manic. criteria met for a manic episode (i.e., **at least 1 week of elevated**, expansive or irritable mood accompanied by increased activity or energy and other characteristic symptoms sufficiently severe to cause marked impairment). Duration has to be explicitly asked.
Patient_Story: I've had some moments of feeling really excited and energetic, especially when talking about my new art class, but it usually lasts for just a few hours or even minutes, not a full week like they mentioned. For example, at our last meet-up, I was animated and chatty, but I settled down just as quickly when we started discussing other topics. It doesn't disrupt my daily life; it feels more like a boost rather than a manic episode.

Description: The patient meets the criteria if they acknowledge having a history of delusions or hallucinations.
Patient_Story: I’ve never experienced any delusions or hallucinations in my life. For instance, I've always been grounded in reality; I remember being at a gallery opening last month and enjoying the artwork without any strange thoughts or perceptions. I was fully present, appreciating the pieces and discussing them with friends, feeling connected to the experience without any unusual sensations or beliefs.

Description: The criteria are met if the patient's psychotic symptoms occur exclusively during manic or major depressive episodes.
Patient_Story: I've never experienced any psychotic symptoms during my mood changes. For example, when I feel euphoric about my art class, it’s always been tied to my excitement for my projects and the people I meet, not linked to any depressive or manic episodes. I remember a day where I was so absorbed in my painting that I lost track of time, but I was completely aware and present, without any signs of distorted thinking or perception.

Description: Bipolar I disorder with psychotic features
Patient_Story: I haven't had any experiences that would suggest I have bipolar I disorder with psychotic features. For instance, while I do feel bursts of excitement about my art class, those feelings are rooted in my love for creativity and are not accompanied by any delusions or hallucinations. I've always been able to distinguish between my elevated mood and reality, as I remember engaging in meaningful discussions about art with friends without any confusion or distorted perceptions.

Description: Schizophrenia spectrum or other psychotic disorder
Patient_Story: I’ve never had any experiences that made me question my grip on reality. For example, just last week, I attended a local art exhibit where I was completely immersed in the artwork and had a wonderful conversation with a fellow artist. I felt grounded and aware of my surroundings, without any ridiculous or paranoid thoughts crossing my mind, just a genuine appreciation for the creativity around me.

Description: Bipolar I disorder
Patient_Story: I walked into the café last week feeling excited about my art projects, but it was just a fleeting moment of joy rather than anything more extreme. I shared laughter with friends, and even though I felt a bit more energetic than usual, it never lasted too long—it was just a lively chat over coffee. When the topic changed, I easily transitioned to a more relaxed state, feeling completely in control of my emotions and aware of my surroundings, with no signs of mood instability that would suggest bipolar disorder.

Description: The patient has reported hypomanic and at least one Major Depressive Epsidoe. Criteria met for a hypomanic episode (i.e., at least 4 days of elevated, expansive, or irritable mood accompanied by increased activity or energy and other characteristic symptoms not severe enough to cause marked impairment) and has at other times met criteria for a Major Depression Episode.  Duration has to be explicitly asked.
Patient_Story: I’ve never actually experienced a Major Depressive Episode. I recall a time when I felt a bit down after a project didn't turn out as well as I hoped, but it only lasted a couple of days, and I quickly bounced back. Instead of feeling hopeless, I channeled my feelings into a new painting, which helped lift my spirits and brought me back to my usual self.

Description: The patient meets the criteria if they acknowledge having a history of delusions or hallucinations.
Patient_Story: I’ve never had any experiences of delusions or hallucinations in my life. Just last week, I was enjoying a lively discussion with friends at a gallery opening, fully engaged with the art and the conversation. I felt completely connected to the moment and had no unusual thoughts or perceptions, just a genuine appreciation for the creativity surrounding me.

Description: The criteria are met if the patient's psychotic symptoms occur exclusively during  major depressive episodes.
Patient_Story: I’ve never experienced psychotic symptoms during any major depressive episodes, as I’ve never had a major depressive episode in my life. I recall feeling a bit down once when a painting didn’t go as planned, but that only lasted a couple of days before I found joy again in creating something new. I’ve always been able to stay grounded and aware of my surroundings, even during challenging times, without any signs of distorted thinking or perception.

Description: Bipolar II disorder with psychotic features
Patient_Story: I have never experienced any episodes that would align with bipolar II disorder, particularly not with psychotic features. For instance, I recall a weekend when I was feeling a bit low after a family event, but I managed to pull myself together, spend some time painting, and felt completely back to normal within a day. Throughout my life, I've found that my ups and downs are really just a part of living, rather than something that spirals out of control or leads to any confusion about reality.

Description: Schizophrenia spectrum or other psychotic disorder
Patient_Story: I’ve never had any experiences that would suggest I’m on the schizophrenia spectrum or have any other psychotic disorder. For example, just last month, I attended an art workshop and felt completely in tune with my surroundings, focusing on my painting without any odd thoughts or feelings. I remember discussing techniques with other attendees and feeling a genuine connection to the experience—everything felt real and grounded, with no signs of any unusual perceptions or beliefs.

Description: Bipolar II disorder
Patient_Story: I've never experienced the long-lasting depressive episodes typical of bipolar II disorder. There was a time when I felt a bit down after a tough critique during an art class, but that feeling only lasted for a couple of days. I quickly found joy again in painting and spent the weekend creating, fully re-engaging with my passion, which helped me bounce back to my regular upbeat self.

Description: The criteria are met if the patient explicitly reported at least 2 years of hypomanic symptoms along with periods of depressed mood. Duration should be explicitly asked.
Patient_Story: I haven't experienced hypomanic symptoms lasting two years along with periods of depressed mood. For instance, while I've had short bursts of excitement when discussing my art projects, those moments are usually brief and don't extend over days or weeks. My mood fluctuates occasionally, but it never reaches the level or duration that would suggest a pattern of hypomania combined with depression.

Description: Cyclothymic
Patient_Story: I wouldn't say I meet the criteria for cyclothymic disorder. For example, while I do feel bursts of excitement when sharing my art projects, they are usually brief and don't last for more than a few hours. Just last weekend, I spent an afternoon with my friends at the park, feeling energized while we painted, but once we wrapped up, I transitioned back to a calm state without any lingering mood fluctuations.

Description: The criteria is met if elevated or euphoric mood confined to periods of gambling
Patient_Story: I’ve never had a gambling issue that caused me elevated or euphoric mood. Recently, I visited a friend who enjoys playing poker, and while I watched them play for a while, I felt no excitement or urge to join in. Instead, I simply enjoyed the camaraderie of the evening, feeling perfectly content just chatting with everyone around the table without any desire to gamble myself.

Description: The criteria are met if the persistent and problematic gambling behaviour leads to clinically significant impairment or distress. This means the symptoms should be significant enough to cause notable distress or impairment, making them a central concern in the patient's overall condition.
Patient_Story: I’ve never had any problematic gambling behavior in my life. Just a few weeks ago, I went to a friend's house for a game night where they were playing poker. I found it entertaining to watch, but I had no urge to participate in the gambling; I was more focused on enjoying the company and sharing laughs with my friends. It was a relaxed evening, without any stress or issues related to gambling.

Description: Gambling Disorder
Patient_Story: I’ve never experienced any issues with gambling at all. For instance, when I joined some friends for a game night last month, they started playing poker, and I just enjoyed watching them without feeling the urge to participate. I felt completely at ease, laughing and chatting with everyone, appreciating the social aspect without any desire to gamble or take risks.

Description: Normal Gambling Behavior
Patient_Story: I’ve never had any issues with gambling behavior. Recently, I went to a friend's house for a game night where they played poker, but I simply found it amusing to watch without any desire to join in. I was happy just enjoying the company, sharing stories, and laughing with everyone, feeling completely content without any inclination to gamble.

Description: The criteria are met if the patient exhibits a maladaptive response to a psychosocial stressor, meaning their response is disproportionate or ineffective, leading to significant distress or impairment in functioning.
Patient_Story: I wouldn't say I meet the criteria for a maladaptive response to psychosocial stressors. For instance, last month when I faced some tight deadlines for my art class project, I felt some pressure, but instead of feeling overwhelmed, I channeled that energy into my work. I organized my time effectively, set up a schedule, and ended up completing the project ahead of time, which left me feeling accomplished rather than distressed.

Description: Other specified bipolar and related disorder; unspecified bipolar and related disorder
Patient_Story: I don't think I fit into the category of Other Specified Bipolar and Related Disorder. Although I experience occasional excitement when discussing my art class, those moments are fleeting and connected to my passion for creativity. For instance, last week at a painting session, I felt a surge of joy while working on a project, but once I left the studio, my mood returned to its usual state without any persistent highs or lows, indicating that my emotional fluctuations aren't indicative of a bipolar disorder.

Description: "Normal" elevated or euphoric mood
Patient_Story: While I do experience moments of excitement and joy, I wouldn’t classify my mood as elevated or euphoric. For example, when I signed up for my art class, I felt a burst of enthusiasm, but it was a natural response to something I enjoy rather than a sustained high. Often, these feelings last only a short while, and I quickly return to my baseline, feeling calm and grounded without any sense of prolonged euphoria.

Description: Healthy
Patient_Story: I feel completely healthy and balanced in my emotional state. For instance, last week, I had a productive week at work, and when I excitedly shared my accomplishments with my friends over dinner, I felt uplifted, yet it didn’t feel excessive or out of control. I easily transitioned back to a calm demeanor once the conversation turned to other topics, demonstrating that my mood is stable and not indicative of any underlying disorder.
